meeting_header:
Date: 2025-08-12
Time: 15:00 PDT
Duration: ~55 min
Attendees: Maya Chen (Redwood AE), Daniel Park (Redwood SE), Priya Singh (Lumina Head of ML), Tom Alvarez (Eng Manager), Sara Gomez (Security)
summary: Technical deep dive focused on how to place moderation/safety filters in the inference pipeline without regressing latency or throughput. Discussed pre-generation vs post-generation moderation, async offload, lightweight classifier trade-offs, KV cache and batching interactions, and VPC/on-prem deployment considerations.
topics: moderation placement (pre vs post vs async)
transcript: 00:00 Maya Chen: Hey everyone, thanks for joining. Um, short agenda — dive into where we put the safety filters and what the perf hits look like. 00:12 Priya Singh: Thanks Maya. We mostly care about user-facing latency under 300 ms P95 for chat, and also we have strict data residency + SOC2 needs. 00:28 Daniel Park: Great, noted. Quick clarifier — when you say safety filters do you mean both moderation classifiers and the post-generation toxicity rerank? 00:36 Priya Singh: Both. We want to avoid bad outputs reaching clinicians, so we run a fast pre-check and a heavier post-check, but we're worried about duplicate cost and extra token latency. 00:50 Tom Alvarez: Also want to understand batching impacts — we currently batch at 8 on our GPU, and any added CPU step could become a bottleneck. 01:02 Sara Gomez: From security side we prefer everything in VPC or on-prem for PHI, so any external API call for moderation is tricky. 01:12 Maya Chen: Understood. So there are typical patterns: pre-generation lightweight filter that blocks obviously disallowed requests, synchronous post-generation filter to catch subtle cases, and async offload where you let response through conditionally and remediate if needed. 01:29 Daniel Park: Right, and performance-wise pre-gen is cheaper because you only run the filter on the prompt, not the generated tokens — but it can be over-aggressive. Post-gen runs on full output and can be heavier, and if it's synchronous it adds to the total response latency. 01:45 Priya Singh: Can you quantify that? like orders of magnitude? 01:49 Daniel Park: Sure — rough numbers from our internal benchmarks: a lightweight classifier on CPU might be ~10-30 ms per request, a medium rule-based hybrid ~30-80 ms, and an ensemble or heavy transformer-based safety model can be 100+ ms if run on CPU — on GPU you can drop that but then you consume precious GPU cycles and it interacts badly with batching. 02:12 Tom Alvarez: So if we batch at 8 and run a safety model on GPU, does it amortize? 02:18 Daniel Park: It can, but remember batching usually optimizes token generation across requests; safety models often operate on full sequences and may not align with generation batching. Also, if you run safety on GPU, that may block generation queues and hurt throughput for other requests. 02:35 Priya Singh: What about KV cache interactions? We heavily rely on KV cache for long-context continuity. Does running filters change cache behavior? 02:43 Daniel Park: Good question. Pre-filters don't touch KV cache. Post-gen moderation obviously inspects generated tokens; that doesn't change cache contents unless you decide to evict or mark a session. However, an async flow where you allow output and later retract can cause state inconsistencies — e.g., cached KV includes generated tokens that were later flagged. So you need guardrails: don't persist to KV until moderation passes, or implement a soft-commit that only persists after green. 03:10 Priya Singh: Soft-commit sounds safer but adds latency to visible state, right? 03:15 Daniel Park: Yes — commit gating means you might delay downstream context until moderation completes. For interactive flows we often commit prompts immediately for responsiveness but mark the KV entry as provisional and prune if marked unsafe. That requires additional orchestration and complexity. 03:31 Tom Alvarez: About quantization — does running safety models on quantized weights change accuracy much? 03:36 Daniel Park: For many lightweight classifiers, int8 quantization is fine and gives big perf wins. For more nuanced safety models you might see a small drop in accuracy; you need to evaluate on your red-team prompts. We also support mixed precision for safety models — run heavier checks at FP16 on GPU when you need higher recall. 03:54 Priya Singh: Is caching moderation decisions possible? Many prompts repeat (templates). 03:58 Maya Chen: Yes — you can cache moderation outcomes keyed by normalized prompt fingerprint. For privacy you should hash and store minimal metadata. Caching reduces repeated compute but watch TTLs so outdated contexts don't bypass checks. 04:12 Sara Gomez: If we deploy on-prem, can Redwood host the moderation model inside our VPC? 04:18 Maya Chen: Absolutely — we support Private deployment with customer-managed networking. We can package the moderator as a co-located service in your VPC or on-prem GPU pool. 04:27 Daniel Park: Important note: if you colocate the moderator on CPU-only infra for cost reasons, expect higher latencies — which pushes you towards async or pre-filter strategies. 04:39 Priya Singh: Any recommended architecture for our constraints: <300 ms P95, batch size 8, SOC2, on-premable? 04:47 Daniel Park: A hybrid approach: pre-filter lightweight model (CPU, <30 ms) to block clear infractions, run generation on GPU with KV cache warm, then if the post-gen heavy check is needed run it asynchronously on a GPU worker pool; if flagged, trigger remediation flows (retract, notify). For critical replies to clinicians, you might prefer synchronous post-check on a dedicated small GPU pool with reserved capacity to keep latency bounded — Redwood Dedicated can provision this. 05:15 Tom Alvarez: How much overhead does async offload add to throughput? 05:19 Daniel Park: Throughput-wise async offload decouples the heavy check from the critical path, so it preserves P95 latency; however it increases end-to-end cost and requires state management. If a lot of outputs are flagged and need retractions, that complicates user UX. 05:35 Priya Singh: We also use heavy prompt engineering with templates — will that improve cache hit rate and reduce moderation load? 05:40 Daniel Park: Yes normalized templates increase cacheability. If prompts are templated, you can compute fingerprint pre-gen and short-circuit some checks. 05:49 Maya Chen: A gotcha — batching and KV: if you send a batched generate request, per-request pre-filters must run before you form the batch else a bad prompt could leak. So you usually pre-filter per-request, then batch generation. 06:05 Tom Alvarez: Are there recommend models for lightweight pre-filters? 06:08 Daniel Park: We typically recommend a distilled transformer or a keyword/rule-hybrid for pre-filter; examples include small distilled classifiers or even heuristics on top of embeddings. For post-filters, a mid-size transformer with FP16 on GPU or a dedicated CPU-optimized ensemble works. 06:25 Priya Singh: Anything about instrumentation and observability? 06:28 Maya Chen: Yes — Redwood Console exposes per-route latency, token-level breakdown, and you can set alerts on moderation rates or false positive spikes. We'll also surface counts of provisional commits vs final commits. 06:41 Sara Gomez: Auditing — we need immutable logs of moderation decisions for audits. 06:45 Maya Chen: We can write audit logs to your KMS-backed storage and include hash of prompt/response for privacy. 06:52 Tom Alvarez: Any real-world numbers of cost delta? 06:55 Daniel Park: Ballpark: lightweight pre-filter adds negligible token cost but maybe ~0.5-2% overall compute. Synchronous heavy post-filter run on GPU could increase cost by 10-40% depending on hit rate. Async reduces latency cost but not total compute cost. 07:15 Priya Singh: Good. I want to see benchmarks on our exact templates. 07:18 Maya Chen: We'll run the 3-config benchmark and return numbers. 07:22 Daniel Park: We'll include KV warm/cold, batching at 8, and scenarios with quantized safety models. 07:30 Priya Singh: Great, thanks. Last question — are there any pitfalls you commonly see? 07:34 Daniel Park: Yes: 1) persist-then-moderate (leads to inconsistent caches), 2) running heavy checks on shared GPU pool (causes tail latency), 3) relying solely on heuristics that miss corner cases. 07:48 Maya Chen: Okay wrapping — next steps captured in notes, we'll share benchmark plan and security docs. Thanks everyone. 07:54 Priya Singh: Thanks, appreciate it. 07:56 End of call
